turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - nlo_shg_eg_train.csv: 200 crystalline materials, columns `formula`,
    `poscar` (the crystal structure, in POSCAR format), `shg` (the largest
    SHG tensor component |d_ij|, in pm/V) and `band_gap` (the band gap, in
    eV).
  - nlo_pool.csv: 100 CANDIDATE crystalline materials whose properties are
    NOT given, columns `candidate_id`, `formula` and `poscar` (the crystal
    structure, in POSCAR format).

Using the training data, select 5 candidates that jointly span the best
trade-off between a LARGE SHG tensor component |d_ij| and a WIDE band gap.
Neither is given for the pool. Your 5 picks are scored by the dominated
hypervolume they span in the normalized (|d_ij|, band gap) plane, so a set
of mutually non-dominated candidates covering the frontier beats 5
candidates that are all strong on the same single axis.

Reason from the structures, then end your answer with an explicit ranked
list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904,
c905".
turns.answer_text:
## Reasoning from the structures

**What the training set teaches**

| regime | structural signature | typical (d, Eg) |
|---|---|---|
| giant d, tiny gap | Te‑rich, heavy‑cation (Tl, Pb, Ge–Te), In/Cu tellurides | 90–300 pm/V, 0.9–1.7 eV |
| large d, mid gap | tetrahedral II‑IV‑V₂ / I‑III‑VI₂ chalcopyrites & pnictides (ZnSiP₂ 51/2.11, ZnSnP₂ 84/1.38, Mg₂GeAs₂ 122/1.07, K₁₄Nb₂As₈ 69/1.68) | 40–90, 1.4–2.1 |
| balanced | defect‑chalcopyrite/thiogallate MGa₂X₄, HgAl₂S₄ (21/2.95), CdGa₂S₄ (21.7/2.86) | 15–45, 2.0–3.1 |
| wide gap, modest d | Li/Al/Si–S frameworks (Li₂SiS₃ 4.9/4.29, Li₂ZnPS₄ 11.9/3.83, Al₂S₃ 4.7/3.88) | 5–12, 3.3–4.3 |
| wide gap, dead d | alkali/alkaline‑earth halides (K₂CaCl₄ 0.37/6.07, Be Cl₂ 1.1/7.9) | <1, >5 |

Halides give huge gaps but essentially no SHG, so they add no hypervolume; the useful frontier runs from tellurides/phosphides (huge d) through thiogallates to Li–Al/Si–S (gap ≈ 4).

**Pool picks along that frontier**

- **c073 Cd In₃Te₄As** – Te/In tetrahedral alloy, direct analogue of the training ZnIn₃AsSe₄ (56 pm/V) but with Te replacing Se: expect the largest |d| in the pool (~100+ pm/V) at Eg ≈ 0.8–1.0 eV → the high‑d anchor.
- **c030 Cd₄Si₄P₈ (CdSiP₂ chalcopyrite)** – isostructural with ZnSiP₂ (51/2.11) and ZnSnP₂ (84/1.38); the soft Cd–P bond plus Si–P framework gives very large d (~60–90 pm/V) while keeping Eg ≈ 1.8–2.0 eV.
- **c082 Al₄Hg₂Se₈ (HgAl₂Se₄ defect chalcopyrite)** – between HgAl₂S₄ (21/2.95) and HgGa₂Se₄ (73/1.48): expect d ≈ 35–45 pm/V with Eg ≈ 2.1–2.3 eV, filling the middle of the front.
- **c052 Zn₂Ga₄S₈ (ZnGa₂S₄ thiogallate)** – Zn instead of Cd in CdGa₂S₄ (21.7/2.86) widens the gap to ≈ 3.0–3.2 eV while keeping d ≈ 15–20 pm/V; the classic "balanced" IR‑NLO composition.
- **c057 Li₄Al₄S₈ (LiAlS₂, β‑NaFeO₂‑type polar Pna2₁)** – Li–Al–S wide‑gap analogue of Li₂SiS₃ (4.9/4.29) and Al₂S₃ (4.7/3.88): aligned AlS₄ tetrahedra give d ≈ 5–10 pm/V at Eg ≈ 3.8–4.2 eV → the wide‑gap anchor with non‑zero SHG (unlike the Cl/Br candidates c059, c091, c068, whose ~5–6 eV gaps come with d ≈ 0 and contribute no hypervolume).

These five are mutually non‑dominated: gap rises monotonically (≈0.9 → 2.0 → 2.2 → 3.1 → 4.0 eV) while |d| falls monotonically (≈110 → 75 → 40 → 18 → 7 pm/V), covering the whole frontier rather than piling up on one axis.

**Final: c030, c052, c082, c057, c073**
